title.en: Advance the solver on a fixed step

summary: Integrate physics on a fixed timestep decoupled from rendering, and interpolate for display.
objective: Make simulated behaviour reproducible and stable regardless of frame rate.
applies_when: A solver advances state over time in an interactive scene.
The scene can be paused, slowed, or run on machines of different speed.
A demonstration must repeat identically for comparison.
intent_signals: the simulation behaves differently each run
it explodes on a slow machine
example_prompts: Make the physics demonstration repeat identically each time.
Add slow motion without changing the reported physics.
negative_signals: Purely kinematic animation driven by elapsed time with no solver.
Analytic solutions evaluated directly at a time value.
not_for: Purely kinematic animation driven by elapsed time with no solver.
Analytic solutions evaluated directly at a time value.

principles: Driving a solver with the frame interval makes the result depend on the machine, the window and the moment, so the same demonstration produces different outcomes and cannot be discussed.

The step size is a numerical parameter: a typical engine default is one sixtieth of a second, smaller steps give better accuracy, and large steps worsen the approximations in the equations of motion and can miss collisions entirely.
Fixed-step integration with an accumulator separates simulation time from display time, which is what makes pause, slow motion and replay meaningful.
Slow motion must scale simulation time, not the reported physical quantities; velocities and forces stay in model units regardless of playback rate.
implementation: Accumulate elapsed real time and run whole fixed steps, carrying the remainder, then interpolate rendering between the last two states.

Cap the number of steps per frame and state the policy when the cap is hit: carry the remainder, drop simulation time, or pause. Schedule inputs on the simulation clock rather than on frame arrival, or throttling will change the run even with fixed steps.
Expose the step size and note it with the artifact, since it is part of the model rather than a rendering detail.
Seed any randomness explicitly and keep the input sequence recorded when reproducibility is claimed.
Report physical quantities in model units and show the playback rate separately.
observable_checks: Run the same complete configuration twice, comparing states at equal simulation times with a stated numerical criterion. Divergence shows non-reproducibility, not its cause: unrecorded input timing, unseeded randomness, uninitialised state, solver ordering or platform arithmetic all produce it, and fixed stepping alone does not exclude them.
Throttle the frame rate deliberately and confirm the outcome is unchanged.
Switch to slow motion and confirm reported velocities and forces are unchanged while the motion appears slower.

Reduce the step size and compare: a converging result supports the current choice, while a qualitative change is evidence to investigate, often a missed impact now resolved or genuinely sensitive dynamics, rather than proof that refinement is wrong.

creative_affordances: Dramatic time effects such as slow motion, freeze and rewind are entirely compatible with a fixed step.
A deliberately coarse step can be shown as a teaching device about numerical error.
Adaptive integration is legitimate when it is deterministic and reproducible; the requirement is a defined relationship between simulation time and display time, not one fixed number.
known_limits: Authored simulation guidance citing documented timestep behaviour of one engine; no simulation has been run or benchmarked for this record.
Full determinism across platforms also depends on floating-point behaviour, which this rule does not guarantee.

claims.statement: The simulation timestep of a rigid-body engine controls how far the physics state is integrated each step, with a typical default of one sixtieth of a second; smaller timesteps yield better accuracy, while large timesteps increase the effect of the linearisation approximations in the equations of motion and may result in missed collisions.
claims.scope: Documented behaviour of one rigid-body engine; the numerical accuracy of a specific simulation is not claimed.

source_refs.locator: dt default, accuracy with smaller timesteps and consequences of large timesteps
